payload.description: Prediction stamping moved from one config per night (the top-ranked config) to every mc_passed config across all three assets, with no selection step between what the system evaluates and what enters the record. Meta-model graduation (META_MIN_SAMPLES) now counts distinct settle dates rather than raw labeled rows, because multiple same-night configs are correlated and carry roughly one night of information between them, not one row of information each. This increases stamped rows per night from ~1 to ~6. Purpose: remove operator discretion over which configs get graded, and accelerate corpus accumulation toward the meta-model's training threshold. No change to strategy logic, MC/WFO gating, or the 7-day hold period.

Disclosure: a network outage caused the Binance price fetch to fail for all three assets (BTC/USDT, ETH/USDT, SOL/USDT) on 2026-07-31 and 2026-08-01. At that time, the pipeline's price loader silently substituted a synthetic fallback price series and continued rather than aborting, so that night's walk-forward optimisation and Monte Carlo gating both ran on fabricated prices, not real market data. The 16 predictions stamped on 2026-07-31 and the 21 stamped on 2026-08-01 have entry prices that were never real market prices and must not be treated as real predictions. The synthetic series was seeded on asset name only, with no date component, so it was fully deterministic per asset: 2026-07-31 and 2026-08-01 replayed an identical fabricated price history rather than being two independent degraded nights. This fallback has since been removed: a Binance fetch failure now aborts the cycle and publishes a PIPELINE_FAILURE entry instead of proceeding on invented data. Fix commit: caf8a4986c61f3fead93ef6d9e52930bca5feda2. The affected prediction rows in reports/predictions.jsonl have not been deleted or altered; they remain in the record with this entry as the correction.

See METHODOLOGY_CHANGE entry a39455b63283c7780a30d4a23adfc03e7543f83ab70215518135c9a9f05d21d7 for the full incident disclosure and fix commit caf8a4986c61f3fead93ef6d9e52930bca5feda2.

payload.description: Disclosure: LiveMonitor.register() has never been called anywhere in the nightly pipeline since it was introduced in the system's initial commit, 607da1ffc2685d64e4252e401f7b0196df029465 ("Add Alfie Night Shift — 7-stage autonomous overnight cycle", 2026-06-18). LiveMonitor.__init__ sets self._active = {}, and across every commit since, the only method ever called on it from cycle.py is deregister() (Stage 7's auto-suspend branch); register() has no call site in the codebase's history. Consequences, verified against the live database: (1) Stage 2's collect_pending_outcomes() reads self.monitor.live_performance_snapshot(), which iterates self._active and is therefore always empty, so update_live_outcome() is never reached from the real nightly path. Zero of the 154 real rows currently in corpus.db have ever received a survived or decay_ratio label. (2) Stage 7's check_all() iterates the same always-empty self._active, so the decay-ratio and drawdown-based early-stop logic in LiveMonitor.check() has never run on a real config, zero rows have ever been written to the live_monitor table, and the auto-suspend branch in cycle.py has never fired. (3) Because meta-model graduation requires META_MIN_SAMPLES=30 distinct labeled dates, and no real row has ever carried a survived/decay_ratio label, the meta-model has never trained on real data under this code path -- no meta_model.pkl produced from real data has ever existed. The only training that has ever occurred used 60 fully synthetic DEMO_* rows seeded by run_nightshift.py --demo, which write survived/decay_ratio directly via insert_config_entry/update_live_outcome and bypass LiveMonitor entirely; those rows are not part of the real corpus and were never claimed as such. Since inception, README.md described Stage 2 as pulling 'results from live-monitored configs' and Stage 7 as performing 'decay checks, auto-suspend' -- both stated as active, ongoing pipeline behaviour. Neither has ever executed, from the first night this system ran through today. This entry is disclosure only: register() has not been wired in as part of this entry, and no corpus rows, briefs, or predictions have been altered. The README is being corrected separately to describe what actually runs. Defect introduced in commit 607da1ffc2685d64e4252e401f7b0196df029465 (2026-06-18).

Disclosure: a walk-forward validation defect in nightshift/wfo_engine.py means the WFO/MC 'out-of-sample' figures reported in every brief chained to date are not genuinely out-of-sample. In WFOEngine.optimise() (wfo_engine.py), line 89 sets train_all = prices -- the full ~500-day price series for the asset, not a slice preceding any fold. The Optuna objective (lines 92-98) scores every candidate parameter set with gt_score(self.strategy_fn(train_all, p)), i.e. against that full series, and top_params (lines 104-113) is selected purely by that full-history score. Only after the winning parameter sets are already chosen are they re-evaluated on windowed fold slices drawn from the same underlying series (lines 119-133), and those returns are the ones labelled OOS and fed into sharpe_oos, gt_score_oos, max_dd_oos, sortino_oos, calmar_oos, and win_rate_oos (lines 136-151). Because parameter selection already used performance on the very days later scored as 'out-of-sample,' those days were not held out from selection, and MIN_OOS_SHARPE (the gate at line 141) has been filtering on an inflated metric rather than a genuine holdout Sharpe. Impact: this affects config selection and every WFO/MC metric reported in a brief or written to a corpus row -- every sharpe_oos, gt_score_oos, and max_dd_oos figure chained to date should be read as in-sample-influenced, not as a true holdout result. It does NOT affect the integrity of the record itself: predictions were still stamped before settlement (nightshift/stamp_prediction.py) with a fixed entry price and settle date, and graded after the fact against real Binance closes by a rule fixed in advance and never changed retroactively (nightshift/label_outcomes.py) -- the WIN/LOSS/NO_CALL grading on the chain is unaffected by this defect. This is a methodology defect in how candidate configs are scored and selected, not a tampering or grading-integrity issue. The defect has existed since the system's initial commit, 607da1ffc2685d64e4252e401f7b0196df029465 ('Add Alfie Night Shift -- 7-stage autonomous overnight cycle', 2026-06-18), and is present in every WFO run since. This entry is disclosure only -- the objective in wfo_engine.py has not been changed as part of this entry, and no corpus rows, briefs, or predictions have been altered. README.md's Stage 4 description is being corrected separately to reflect that the reported OOS metrics are not currently genuine holdout results.

Disclosure: the first AUDIT_RESULT entry chained by nightshift/self_audit.py (entry 21, published 2026-08-01T17:14:54Z) reports an incorrect finding_count for the calendar_coverage check. That check passed with zero findings, but the entry records finding_count: 2. Cause: the _finding_count() helper summed the length of every list in a check's detail{} dict, which included calendar_coverage's two-element 'range' metadata field ([start_date, end_date]) alongside genuine finding lists. The chained summary therefore attributed two findings to a check that found nothing. The full report file on disk (reports/audit/audit_20260801.json, sha256 1ae4d9332a33159abc3372f02f361581101f370211da7ce7a6b3bc528b768e45, referenced by that entry) was always correct and shows gap_dates: [] -- only the summary count inside the chained payload is wrong. Impact: cosmetic and confined to that one field in that one entry. No check result, status, or finding was altered or suppressed; overall_status FAIL was correct and driven by the four checks that genuinely failed. Fix: _finding_count() now counts only an explicit FINDING_KEYS allowlist, so metadata fields cannot inflate a count; verified to report 0 for calendar_coverage. Entry 21 is left on the chain unaltered rather than removed. It had not been pushed at the time the error was found and could have been truncated as the last line without breaking any downstream hash, but removing a locally-held entry because it contained an embarrassing number is the practice this record exists to rule out -- README.md states there is no filtering hook in the publisher, and that claim is about practice as much as code. Separately, self_audit.py's invocation in run_and_publish.sh has been moved from after the pipeline to before all early-exit guards. As originally wired it ran only on nights the cycle completed cleanly, so the calendar-gap check could never observe a failed or aborted night -- the inverse of its purpose. check_calendar_coverage() now walks from genesis to yesterday rather than today, since the audit runs before tonight's brief is chained and counting today would report a false gap every night.

payload.description: Change to how the meta-model is trained, and to how configs are identified. Both defects were found by inspecting the data, not the design, and both are disclosed here before any model has been trained on the affected path. (1) config_id was positional rather than identifying. WFOEngine.optimise() assigned f'{asset}_{family}_{idx:04d}' where idx was the row's index in that night's results list, so the same config_id string named different parameter sets on different nights. Measured 2026-08-02 against corpus.db: 29 config_ids appear on more than one deployment_date, and 28 of those 29 carry different params_json across those dates. Any logic reasoning about a config across nights -- decay tracking, joining corpus features to graded prediction outcomes, or LiveMonitor.register() -- was therefore comparing unrelated strategies that happened to occupy the same list slot. config_id is now sha256 over (asset, family, sorted params), so identical parameters always produce an identical id and distinct parameters never collide. Rows written before this change keep their positional ids and have not been rewritten; joins remain scoped by (config_id, deployment_date) so they stay correct across the boundary. (2) The meta-model's two training targets both derived from wfo_sharpe. 'survived' was defined as (live_sharpe_20d / wfo_sharpe) >= META_SURVIVE_THRESHOLD and 'decay_ratio' was that same ratio, and wfo_sharpe is sharpe_oos -- the metric disclosed in the 2026-08-01 METHODOLOGY_CHANGE as in-sample-influenced because parameter selection in WFOEngine.optimise() uses the full price series later scored as out-of-sample. Training a classifier on those targets would have taught it to predict whether forward performance reached half of a number this record has already published as inflated. Separately, both targets required LiveMonitor to accumulate daily returns across nights, which it structurally could not: LiveMonitor._active is an in-memory dict on a nightly batch process that exits after minutes, and is reconstructed empty on every run, so register() could not have produced a label even had it been called. The targets are now outcome_win (WIN=1, LOSS=0) and outcome_return_pct (realised 7-day return), read from reports/predictions.jsonl and joined to corpus features on (config_id, cycle_date). That label is produced by label_outcomes.py, graded against real Binance daily closes by a rule fixed in advance and never changed retroactively, and is already chained as LABELED_OUTCOME entries. It depends on no WFO metric. The join was verified exact: all 55 stamped predictions match a corpus row. NO_CALL predictions remain excluded, as everywhere else. Training is additionally refused while every labeled row shares a single outcome class, a state a small early corpus can easily reach and which would yield a model that appears perfect and means nothing. Consequence and remaining limitation: the WFO look-ahead defect still biases wfo_sharpe, wfo_gt_score and wfo_max_dd as INPUT FEATURES to the meta-model, but no longer corrupts the training LABEL. That defect remains disclosed and unfixed, and it no longer blocks meta-model graduation. Graduation still requires 30 distinct settle dates carrying a WIN or LOSS; as of this entry there are 0, with 54 predictions in flight settling from 2026-08-03 onward. The meta-model remains in [FALLBACK] and ranks by GT-Score. Also noted for correction: the README states the prediction stamper emits only 'long' or 'none', but the record contains a third value, 'neutral'. The README is wrong on that point and will be corrected separately.

New strategy family added to the nightly pipeline: 'breakout', a long-only Donchian channel breakout, implemented in nightshift/strategies/__init__.py and registered in STRATEGY_REGISTRY. Rule: enter long when the close exceeds the highest close of the prior lookback days; exit on a close below the lowest close of the prior exit_lookback days, or after max_hold_days, whichever comes first. Both channel bounds are computed with .shift(1) so the bar being tested is excluded from its own channel. Verified against 500 real BTC/USDT daily bars: the returns array matches the input length with no NaN, 162 of 500 days are in-trade, degenerate parameter values return an all-zero signal rather than raising, and an explicit look-ahead test confirms that truncating the final 40 bars leaves every earlier return identical -- no future bar influences a past signal. Why it was added, stated plainly so the reason is on the record and not inferred later: REGIME_FAMILY_GATE has marked 'breakout' eligible in regime 0 since the system's initial commit 607da1f while STRATEGY_REGISTRY never contained it, so the regime gate has been offering a family that could never run. self_audit check 6 reported that mismatch on every run since the audit was introduced; it now passes. The second reason is throughput of gradeable outcomes: across 2026-07-24 to 2026-08-02, 55 configs cleared all five Monte Carlo gates but only 12 (21.8%) had a live entry signal on the night they were stamped, and only 3 of 8 nights produced any gradeable prediction at all. Because meta-model graduation counts distinct settle dates rather than rows, stamping more configs per night cannot accelerate it -- only raising the share of NIGHTS with at least one firing signal can. A breakout entry condition fires on different days than mean reversion or momentum, so adding the family raises that share without weakening any threshold on the three families already present. The alternative considered and rejected was loosening entry thresholds (entry_z, rsi_low) on existing families, which would also have increased signal count but by degrading the quality of the calls entering the record -- optimising the counter at the expense of what the counter is supposed to measure. This family is long-only, like every other strategy here; the stamper still cannot emit 'short'. Limitation carried forward: breakout configs are scored by the same WFOEngine.optimise() path whose out-of-sample metrics remain in-sample-influenced per the 2026-08-01 disclosure, so its reported sharpe_oos and gt_score_oos should be read with the same caution as every other family's. No historical entries, briefs, corpus rows or predictions were altered by this change; it affects future cycles only.

WFO parameter selection rewritten to remove a look-ahead defect. Previously the optimiser scored every candidate on the full price series and then re-scored some of those same days as out-of-sample, so selection and testing overlapped: every wfo_sharpe, gt_score_oos and max_dd_oos published before this entry should be read as in-sample-influenced. From today each fold runs its own search, trained only on data ending 7 days before that fold's test window begins, matching the 7-day prediction hold period. Folds no longer overlap (step moved from 14 days to 28) so no calendar day can enter a parameter set's sample twice, which had been inflating apparent sample size without adding evidence. Each config now records wfo_n_trials and wfo_n_candidates_surviving_min_sharpe, so a reported metric is visibly the best of many trials rather than a single blind result; no deflated-Sharpe correction is applied yet. One thing got worse: param_stability is the spread of a parameter set's scores across folds, and with non-overlapping folds most configs now appear in only one fold, so it reads n/a instead of a number. Boundary: every prediction stamped on or before 2026-08-04, including the BTC/USDT LOSS graded today, came from the old selector and none are being voided. Entry prices were real and the grading rule is unchanged; only which configs got chosen was affected.

PREDICTION STAMPING NARROWED TO LIVE ENTRY SIGNALS ONLY. What changed: until today, stamp() in nightshift/stamp_prediction.py wrote a prediction row for every config that cleared Monte Carlo gating, regardless of whether that config's own entry condition was actually true on tonight's final bar. Because all strategies here are long-only and their entry conditions (RSI below threshold for mean_rev, fast MA above slow MA plus RSI floor for momentum, z-score above entry_z for relative) are usually false on any given night, most stamped rows carried direction none. From today, a gated config with no live entry signal produces no prediction row at all. The condition is logged with its diagnostic and stamp() returns None. Scale of the problem: of 103 rows written to reports/predictions.jsonl to date, 76 had direction none, one was neutral, and 26 were long. Of 57 currently open rows, 43 were direction none. Those rows can only ever grade NO_CALL, which is not an outcome, and they were inflating the apparent activity of the pipeline while producing no evidence about whether any strategy works. Why nothing is lost by not writing them: every config that clears MC gating is already persisted to corpus.db by insert_config_entry at stage 6, before stamping is reached, so the record of what the system considered is unaffected. Non-suppression of nights is separately provable two ways, by the NIGHTLY_BRIEF entry chained every night and by the calendar_coverage check in self_audit.py which fails on any gap. None rows were never the evidence for either claim. What is not being done: reports/predictions.jsonl is not rewritten. All existing none and neutral rows remain exactly as written and will settle and grade NO_CALL through label_outcomes.py unchanged. Nothing published is being edited or removed. Also changed: the module docstring of stamp_prediction.py stated that a row is written for every config that passed gating, which becomes false with this change and has been corrected. And status.py now reports two additional counts alongside metric 2, the raw number of labeled rows and the number of distinct asset, direction and night combinations among them, because several configs agreeing on the same asset on the same night share an entry price and a settle price and therefore grade identically. Those are one unit of evidence, not several, and counting them as several would overstate the corpus. Metric 2 remains the graduation gate and remains the most conservative of the three counts. Honest limitation: this change does not make the system produce more calls. It stops non-calls being recorded as predictions. The underlying rate of genuine directional signals is unchanged, roughly one distinct call every few nights, and 30 labeled outcomes remains far off. The visible counts will get smaller as a result of this entry, not larger. Boundary: predictions stamped on or before 2026-08-08 were written under the old behaviour.

PRE-REGISTRATION OF PRODUCT AND DESIGN CRITERIA, RECORDED BEFORE THE DATA EXISTS. This entry commits in advance to the thresholds by which the project will judge itself, so that the decision cannot later be rationalised toward whatever the record happens to support. PRODUCT CRITERIA, evaluated at 30 distinct labeled calls. One: frequency. A subscription product requires at least 4 distinct calls per month sustained over 90 days. Below that, the subscription form is dead by arithmetic regardless of accuracy. Two: edge. Mean 7-day return of graded calls will be compared against buy-and-hold on the same asset over identical windows. If mean excess return is at or below zero, there is no signals product at any price, and that finding will be published. Three: meta-model value. At graduation its ranking must beat random selection among gated configs on held-out labeled rows, or the learning-system claim is dropped. Four: reader response, measured by engagement with published record entries, not follower count. DESIGN COMMITMENTS. Night Shift will add a context_hash, SHA-256 over the exact OHLCV window used, to every stamped prediction, so a reader can verify the input data and not only that the output was not edited. Day Shift, when it begins, inherits three constraints fixed now: its universe will be constructed from point-in-time index membership as of each historical date and never from a present-day list, because selecting todays large-caps embeds survivorship bias at the universe level; it will use adjusted close with the adjustment method and data provider named explicitly in its genesis entry, because providers disagree and an unstated method is unauditable; and it will carry context_hash from its first entry. LIMITS ACKNOWLEDGED IN ADVANCE. Sample starvation is not a defect but a tradeoff: at the current rate of roughly one distinct call every few nights, a statistically meaningful result is years away, and increasing sample size would require more assets, shorter holds, or more strategy families, each of which trades per-call quality for statistical power. That tradeoff has not been made and will be published if it is. Selection across forecasters cannot be solved from inside this record: if many parties publish honest verified records, the best-looking one is probably lucky, so N will always be published alongside any performance claim. Verification itself is not a moat. At least four independent parties shipped comparable pre-commitment proof systems during 2026. The durable asset is record length and disclosure quality, both of which accrue only with time.

INPUT DATA IS NOW COMMITTED ALONGSIDE THE PREDICTION, AND A GAP IN THE RECORD IS DISCLOSED. Every stamped prediction now carries context_hash, a SHA-256 over the OHLCV window the prediction was made against, together with context_source, context_start, context_end and context_n_bars recorded in the clear. Until now the chain proved that a prediction was committed before its outcome and had not been edited afterward, but said nothing about the price data behind it - that data was fetched by this system and never independently checkable. A reader can now re-fetch the same named date range from the same source and recompute the hash. Only closed bars are hashed. The final bar in each fetched window is the current in-progress daily candle, whose values keep changing until the UTC day ends, so including it would make context_hash permanently unreproducible by anyone. The rule for deciding whether a bar is closed has been moved to core/bar_calendar.py and is now called by both the stamper and the grader, so the two cannot drift apart on what final means. That rule assumes UTC-midnight daily closes, which is correct for continuously traded crypto and wrong for equities, and is documented as such. Predictions written before today carry no context field. SEPARATELY DISCLOSED, NOT YET FIXED: reports/predictions.jsonl has no integrity protection of its own. The hash chain covers chain.jsonl only. Stamped predictions are protected solely by the nightly git commit, and the cycle writes them hours before that commit runs, leaving a window in which loss or truncation would be unrecoverable and undetected - the nightly self-audit does not read predictions.jsonl at all. Tonight that window was demonstrated: an automated tool deleted the file during testing, and it was recoverable only because a commit happened to precede the deletion. Nothing was lost and the file was verified intact at 113 rows spanning 2026-07-24 to 2026-08-11. The most valuable artifact this system produces, claims committed before their outcomes exist, currently has the weakest protection in the repository. This is a disclosure, not a fix.

payload.description: PREDICTIONS FILE IS NOW COVERED BY THE CHAIN. Every chain entry from this point carries predictions_n and predictions_sha256, the row count and SHA-256 of reports/predictions.jsonl at the moment that entry was published. Until now the hash chain protected chain.jsonl only. Stamped predictions, which are the claims this system exists to commit before their outcomes are known, were protected solely by the nightly git commit, leaving a window in which deletion or truncation would have been both unrecoverable and undetected. That gap was disclosed in chain entry 70 as a disclosure and not a fix. This is the fix. A seventh self-audit check now fails if predictions_n ever decreases between two chain entries. The file is append-only in practice: stamp_prediction.py only appends, and label_outcomes.py and void_predictions.py both rewrite the same parsed rows back to disk, grading or voiding in place, so the hash legitimately changes between entries but the count must never fall. Both were read to confirm this before the check was relied on. What this still does not catch: an edit that preserves the row count changes predictions_sha256 without changing predictions_n, and the check compares counts only, so it detects deletion and truncation but not substitution. That limitation is recorded in the self-audit module's own list of what it cannot catch. Chain entries published before today carry no such field and are skipped by the check rather than compared against newer ones.

Re-publishing the pre-registered product criteria in structured, machine-readable form. Entry 3c2ee64d published these thresholds as prose on 2026-08-11; the chain is append-only, so that entry cannot be amended to carry structured data, and status.py had to hand-transcribe the numbers into constants with a comment admitting the link was unverifiable. The values are unchanged - only their form. From this entry forward status.py resolves them from the chain itself and states which fields came from the chain and which fell back to hardcoded defaults. The prose entry remains authoritative for the two criteria that are not numeric thresholds - edge versus buy-and-hold, and meta-model ranking versus random - which are not expressible as constants.

CORRECTING THE HEADLINE FIGURE THE PUBLIC VERIFY COMMAND REPORTS. Until today core/verify_chain.py printed outcomes as a count of LABELED_OUTCOME chain entries. Several configs can pass gating on the same asset, direction and night, and each stamps its own prediction with the same entry price and the same settle price, so each produces its own chained outcome entry with the same grade. Counting entries therefore counted one call several times. As of this entry the record shows 4 win entries and 2 loss entries, which is 1 win and 2 losses across 3 distinct calls - the four wins are a single ETH/USDT long from 2026-08-05 that four configs agreed on. Every figure this command printed before today overstated the win side, and anyone who ran it and read 4 wins 2 losses was reading configs in agreement, not calls made. The command now prints distinct calls as the headline and the raw entry count beneath it, labelled as such, using the same asset-direction-night key status.py already uses so the two tools cannot drift. A CONFLICT line now appears if two entries sharing that key ever grade differently, so a contradiction cannot be silently absorbed into the headline. Per-config rows are kept deliberately: the meta-model needs to learn which configs to trust, which requires per-config outcomes. Nothing in the record is being rewritten - only how it is summarised.

payload.description: Correction to the 2026-09-14 strategy freeze (chain entry 234). That freeze was declared against code_version -- the git HEAD sha at chain time -- which moves on every commit, including the tooling/infra commits the freeze itself explicitly permits (disclosed on-chain before the fix, per the disclose-before-fix rule). code_version therefore cannot actually distinguish a permitted infrastructure fix from a prohibited change to signal logic, strategy parameters, feature set, gating thresholds, or model architecture: a logging tweak moves it exactly as much as a real strategy change would. That defect went unnoticed until now -- nothing forced the two to disagree in the two nights since 234, but they were never the same claim, and the freeze was resting on the wrong one. The chain is append-only, so entry 234 cannot be amended; this entry corrects it going forward instead. The freeze is repointed to strategy_version -- a sha256 content hash over exactly the files that can change what signal gets emitted (nightshift/strategy_version.py: config.py, cycle.py, mc_gate.py, regime_engine.py, stamp_prediction.py, strategies/__init__.py, wfo_engine.py), computed from file contents, independent of git history, so a tooling-only commit made during the freeze no longer moves it. Both values, named: the original code_version was 0632a1ddb5e989b1725d2f29bb80b02eb3903b8b (first seen entry 223; core/verify_chain.py keeps tracking it as FROZEN_CODE_VERSION, and the 3 losses already chained under it stay on the record as real history, not erased). The repointed strategy_version is a7bdda9ce2654c0d24810b86c27c6e427b9f9aac7258ce98b5b8289acf3e79fb (FROZEN_STRATEGY_VERSION) -- this is the value that governs the freeze from this entry forward. Every other term of entry 234 is unchanged: what is permitted and prohibited during the freeze, the disclose-before-fix rule, and the lift condition of 30 distinct labeled dates -- now measured against strategy_version, not code_version.

payload.description: Two things, disclosed together: infra fixes just made under the freeze, and a limitation of the safeguard that watches for silent gaps. Infra fixes (permitted during the freeze -- infrastructure fixes, bug fixes, logging -- per entry 234; none of the three touch the strategy_version surface, so strategy_version is unchanged by this entry): (1) run_and_publish.sh no longer gates cycle execution on GitHub reachability -- the cycle now always runs, and a network-down condition is caught downstream as a normal cycle failure instead of pre-empting the attempt entirely; 11 of the 12 PIPELINE_FAILURE entries to date came from that removed pre-check. (2) PIPELINE_FAILURE payloads now carry failure_class and exception_type (new entries only, no backfill) -- coarse categories, not a traceback, enough to tell an upstream data outage from a bug in our own code. (3) watchdog.py now alerts when the entry chained that night exists and is pushed but is itself a PIPELINE_FAILURE, rather than logging OK -- previously a cleanly-chained failure was indistinguishable from a clean night in the alerting path. Known limitation, stated plainly: the watchdog (com.alfie.nightshift.watchdog, launchd, 06:30 IST) is a job on the same machine as the pipeline it watches, subject to the identical awake-constraint. If the laptop is off or asleep through the entire attempt window, neither the pipeline nor the watchdog fires, and nothing gets chained and nothing alerts -- the watchdog cannot watch for its own absence. The only alert channel that exists is a local macOS notification (osascript), which requires notification permissions the code has no way to verify are actually granted, and which is only seen by someone physically at or near this Mac. There is no off-machine channel -- no email, no SMS, no push to a phone. In practice the watchdog has fired every night since 2026-08-27 with no gaps, but that is an empirical track record, not a structural guarantee, and the structural gap is real regardless of how it has behaved so far.

payload.description: Two things, disclosed together, both permitted-during-freeze categories per entry 234 (verifier changes; anchoring changes): what OpenTimestamps anchoring proves and does not prove, and the anchoring + verifier changes just made. What anchoring proves: that a specific chain entry existed at or before a specific point in time, bounded by the Bitcoin block a calendar attestation lands in. Nothing more. It does not prove the entry is older than that block -- it bounds one side only, the same honest limit the README has stated since anchoring began. Above all, it does not prove the call recorded in that entry was any good: not that the signal was correct, not that the strategy is sound, not that the return was real money. Anchoring is a claim about the timeline of the record, not about the merit of the record -- those are different questions, and a reader should not come away from a verified receipt believing anything about the second one. payload.description: Four-night publishing outage, 2026-09-17 to 2026-09-19, and why the backstop built to catch exactly this did not surface it. The GitHub credential used for git push (alfie-workflow-token, embedded in the origin remote URL) expired around 2026-09-17. Entries 252-255 -- self-audit and brief for both 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-19 -- were chained locally on schedule, correctly hashed, correctly OTS-stamped, but never reached origin: git push failed all 3 retries each night. Confirmed live and reproducible: a direct push attempt returned HTTP 401 on git-receive-pack, and the GitHub REST API returned {"message":"Bad credentials"} for the same token -- not a network blip, the credential itself was dead. The chain's own watchdog (nightshift/watchdog.py, launchd, 06:30 IST) is designed to catch precisely an unpushed-but-chained night: it did, both nights, correctly. unpushed_commits() detected HEAD diverging from the tracked upstream ref, its own independent push retry failed and captured the real git error, and watchdog.log received an accurate, detailed ALERT line each morning naming the exact failure. The gap was not detection -- it was notification. watchdog.py's alert() has exactly one delivery path, a local macOS notification via osascript, called with check=False and no captured output; that transport returns exit 0 regardless of whether the OS actually displayed anything, so a delivery failure is invisible to the code that called it. A forensic check of this Mac's own notification-permission record (~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.ncprefs.plist) found no entry at all for osascript, python3, Terminal, or Script Editor -- no permission grant on record for the sender identity this alert path posts under. The practical reading is that these notifications have likely never been delivered, not only during this outage: the watchdog was correctly diagnosing bad nights and writing the truth to a log file nobody was prompted to open. This corrects, rather than merely restates, a claim made at chain entry 239 (2026-09-15), which disclosed the same structural risk in advance and characterized the channel as having "fired every night since 2026-08-27 with no observed gaps -- an empirical track record, not a structural guarantee." That track record measured whether the watchdog ran and logged correctly, which it did, consistently -- not whether the operator was ever actually notified, which the evidence here suggests was false the entire time. Those are not the same claim, and entry 239 conflated them. Resolution: the token was rotated, the remote was switched from a URL-embedded credential to an osxkeychain credential helper (removing a second problem along the way -- the dead token had been sitting in plaintext in .git/config and, via git's own error output, in nightshift/logs/watchdog.log), and all 4 outstanding commits were pushed and verified against the live remote tip. core/verify_chain.py confirms CHAIN VALID, 255 entries unbroken from genesis, OTS receipts 245/245 with 0 missing and 0 invalid. What is not resolved, stated plainly rather than left to be inferred from its absence here: the alert channel itself is unchanged. It is still local-machine-only, still has no verifiable delivery, still has no off-machine backup -- the exact gap entry 239 named is still open as of this entry's publication. A future entry that replaces or hardens this channel should reference this one.

payload.description: Infra fix disclosed, per the freeze's disclose-before-fix rule: watchdog.py's alert() no longer relies solely on a local macOS notification whose delivery it never checked. Entry 256 disclosed that alert()'s only channel was osascript, called with its result discarded, and that a forensic check of this Mac's notification-permission record found no grant on file for that sender at all -- meaning delivery had likely been silently failing since the watchdog was first set up, not only during the 4-night outage that prompted the check. This entry discloses the fix, implemented against four explicit constraints: off-machine (must reach the operator without them being at this Mac), zero recurring cost, checkable delivery (the watchdog must be able to log whether the alert actually went out), and independence from the GitHub credential this same watchdog checks the health of. alert() now delivers primarily via a new notify_offmachine() function: a single stdlib urllib HTTPS POST to ntfy.sh, a free public push-notification relay, with the HTTP response read back and logged either way -- "ntfy delivered -- HTTP 200" or an explicit failure line, never silence. Local osascript notification still fires afterward as a harmless bonus when it happens to work, but is no longer the sole channel and its result is never logged as if it were reliable. A real bug surfaced during testing and is disclosed here rather than smoothed over: the first implementation used the `str | None` union syntax, which requires Python 3.10+, but launchd invokes this script via this Mac's system /usr/bin/python3, which is 3.9.6 -- not this repo's venv, which does have a newer interpreter. Had this shipped as written, the nightly watchdog run would have crashed on import, invisibly, into watchdog_launchd.log, a file nobody was prompted to check -- the exact same silent-failure shape entry 256 exists to disclose, just relocated to a different line of code. Caught before publish by testing under the actual launchd interpreter rather than the venv one; fixed with `from __future__ import annotations`, and the whole implementation was kept deliberately stdlib-only (a small hand-written .env line-parser instead of python-dotenv, urllib instead of requests) for the identical system-python-vs-venv reason. Verified end to end under /usr/bin/python3: a live ntfy push was sent and delivered (HTTP 200, confirmed in watchdog.log), and a simulated missing-NTFY_TOPIC configuration was confirmed to log as an explicit failure rather than fail silently. NTFY_TOPIC lives in .env, gitignored and untracked -- this repository is public, confirmed by an earlier unauthenticated API check returning 200, so no secret belongs in a tracked file. This entry corrects, in part, the remaining_exposure field of entry 256: off-machine delivery and checkable logging are now addressed. What is not yet addressed, stated plainly: credential-expiry warning is a separate, not-yet-implemented task, and ntfy.sh itself is a single third-party service -- this substitutes one point of failure for a different, off-machine one, it does not eliminate the category. payload.description: Infra fix disclosed, per the freeze's disclose-before-fix rule: watchdog.py now checks the GitHub push credential's expiry every night, closing the last open item entry 257 named as unaddressed. The outage entries 256 and 257 covered was a dead push credential, discovered only because someone happened to look -- four nights after it actually broke. check_credential_expiry() makes one GET https://api.github.com/user with the same credential git push uses and reads GitHub's own github-authentication-token-expiration response header, at negligible cost against a 5,000/hour limit. It distinguishes four outcomes on purpose, because collapsing them into one generic alert would hide which one is true: 'dead' means GitHub rejected the credential right now, with a 401 -- push is already broken tonight, not at some future date; 'warn' means the credential is valid but expires within ten days; 'ok' means neither; 'unknown' means the check itself could not run -- no credential found in the keychain, the GitHub API unreachable, rate-limited, an unexpected response, or a 200 response missing the expected header -- and is logged with the specific reason rather than being silently treated as if it meant "nothing to report." That distinction matters because 'unknown' read as 'ok' would recreate, in the credential check itself, the exact invisible-failure shape entry 256 disclosed in the old alert path: a safeguard that quietly stops being able to tell you anything is not the same as a safeguard confirming there's nothing to tell. Every outcome other than 'ok' is both logged and alerted through notify_offmachine(), the off-machine channel entry 257 added, with wording specific to which of the three problem states applies. The check runs unconditionally at the start of every watchdog invocation, independent of whatever else that night's pipeline did, and folds into the exit code, so a clean brief on a night when the credential is dying still exits non-zero. The credential itself is never written to disk a second time: it is read fresh each run via `git credential fill`, the same osxkeychain helper git push already relies on, held in memory only for the one API call, and discarded -- no new file, no second copy in .env, nothing that would widen where this secret lives. That constraint was treated as binding rather than a nice-to-have; the fix does not exist if it means writing the token somewhere new. Tested under /usr/bin/python3, the actual launchd interpreter, not this repo's venv, matching the standard set at entry 257: a live run against the real, valid credential correctly reported 90.0 days remaining; a live call against the dead 2026-09-17 token correctly returned a 401-based 'dead' result, distinct from a warning; simulated no-credential, unreachable-API, and missing-header cases all correctly returned 'unknown' with a specific reason rather than silently passing as 'ok'; a simulated eight-day-remaining case correctly produced warn-specific wording; both the dead and warn paths were confirmed to route through notify_offmachine() with real ntfy deliveries logged; and a full, unmocked run of watchdog.py's main() completed end to end with exit 0 and the expected log lines. This closes the item entry 257 left open under corrects. What remains open, stated plainly rather than left to be inferred: ntfy.sh is still a single third-party relay, substituted for the prior single point of failure rather than eliminating the category, and this check covers only the GitHub push credential -- it says nothing about other ways the nightly pipeline could fail silently. payload.description:
Correction to the code_dirty field published alongside every chain entry's code_version. code_dirty is meant to tell a reader whether the entry was produced by committed, versioned code or by an uncommitted edit nobody can reconstruct -- a provenance claim, same category as code_version itself. It did not measure that. nightshift/publish_chain.py's _code_version() ran `git status --porcelain` over the entire working tree, with no path scoping, at the moment append_entry() is called during a publish. In run_and_publish.sh's sequence, that moment always falls after cycle.py, label_outcomes.py and void_predictions.py have already written tonight's brief, reports/predictions.jsonl, reports/chain.jsonl and the OTS receipt files to disk, and always before the script's own end-of-run `git add`/`git commit` stages any of it. Those freshly-written, not-yet-staged output files are exactly what git status was seeing and calling "dirty". The field was reporting "a publish is currently in progress" -- true at that instant on essentially every run, regardless of whether a single line of code had changed -- not "this entry came from uncommitted code", which is what code_dirty: true actually claims to a reader.

This was first noticed in chain entries 288-332 (2026-09-28 through 2026-10-03), all 45 of which carry code_dirty: true with no exceptions, during a routine status check. That framing understated the scope. code_version and code_dirty were introduced together at entry 13 (2026-07-29); the very next NIGHTLY_BRIEF, entry 14 (2026-07-30), already carries code_dirty: true, and the pattern has held for nearly the entry's entire existence: of 306 "in-run" entries (NIGHTLY_BRIEF, LABELED_OUTCOME, AUDIT_RESULT, and PIPELINE_FAILURE published through run_and_publish.sh's pipeline), 283 carry code_dirty: true. The 11 that don't are all PIPELINE_FAILURE entries where the cycle crashed before writing any output at all -- those really were clean at the sampling instant, not a gap in the defect. From entry 288 onward there are zero exceptions of either kind: every one of the 45 most recent entries is code_dirty: true.

Root cause is a measurement-ordering defect in the chain's own provenance tooling, not an operator action: _code_version() answers a question about the tree's state using a check that samples that state at a point where the run's own legitimate output is guaranteed to make the answer always true. It is the same class of defect as the brief's labeled-row-count bug corrected earlier in this record -- a value computed at the wrong moment relative to the thing it claims to describe, silently corrupting a provenance or measurement field rather than crashing loudly.

Fixed going forward in commit 85eeeadadba250105e7ca848991378b0c39595b9: _code_version()'s git status call now excludes exactly the paths run_and_publish.sh itself stages at the end of a run (nightshift/briefs/, reports/chain.jsonl, reports/predictions.jsonl, reports/ots/, reports/audit/ -- named RUN_OUTPUT_PATHS, mirrored from that script's three `git add` lines), via git's `:!<path>` exclude pathspec syntax. An alternative of sampling git status once before the pipeline starts and caching the answer for the whole run was considered and rejected: append_entry() is called from several separate process invocations across a single night -- self_audit.py, run_nightshift.py's --failed path, --brief, and the LABELED_OUTCOME/VOID_DECISION publishes from label_outcomes.py/void_predictions.py -- so a pre-run snapshot would need a new cross-process sidecar file to carry it between those processes, which would add exactly the kind of extra moving part this session's own routine status check was independently auditing for (orphaned sidecars), on top of its own staleness-versus-real-time tradeoff against a cached value. payload.description:
Correction to the OTS receipt coverage line printed by core/verify_chain.py. That line reported a single "receipted" count -- 336 -- with a note that the check is structural only. It did not, and could not, distinguish a receipt that is merely calendar-committed (pending) from one actually attested on Bitcoin (confirmed). A reader seeing "336 receipted" had no way to know how much of that number was real Bitcoin attestation versus an unconfirmed calendar promise, and no signal at all that something might be wrong.

Sampling the real chain with the actual `ots` CLI (oldest, middle, and newest receipts, as a routine status check asked) found a real problem: the oldest receipt (2026-07-28) was fully Bitcoin-confirmed on 3 of 4 calendars, as expected, but the middle sample (2026-09-04, 32 days old) had zero Bitcoin attestations on any calendar -- pure PendingAttestation despite being over a month old. A direct `ots upgrade` on that same receipt resolved it instantly from the calendar's own cache, proving the backlog was upgradable, not actually stuck waiting on Bitcoin. A full scan of the chain's 336 receipts found 193 (57%) genuinely still pending, 182 of those older than 48 hours -- far beyond normal Bitcoin confirmation latency (hours, not weeks).

Root cause: nightshift/anchor_ots.py's opportunistic_upgrade(), the nightly backlog-upgrade sweep that already existed and already ran on the same schedule as the rest of anchoring, had a skip-check logic defect: `if "PendingAttestation" not in info.stdout: continue`. A PendingAttestation leaf is written by every `ots stamp` at publish time and is never removed by a later `ots upgrade` -- upgrading only adds a confirmed attestation leaf alongside it, it doesn't replace the original. So "PendingAttestation" is a substring of `ots info`'s output for every real proof, forever, confirmed or not. This condition was therefore never true. Nothing was ever skipped, and every nightly run re-attempted `ots upgrade` against the full candidate list from scratch, oldest-file-modification-time first, inside a fixed 30-second total budget -- spending nearly all of that budget re-verifying the already-confirmed prefix of the list before ever reaching a genuinely pending entry further back.

This was already independently detected, just not fixed or surfaced here: self_audit.py's own ots_proof_coverage check -- different code, written correctly from the start, checking for the presence of a confirmed attestation rather than the absence of a pending one -- has reported FAIL every single day since 2026-08-01, with its finding_count climbing almost monotonically from 4 to 191 over 66 days. Detection worked the entire time. Remediation (the upgrade sweep) did not. And verify_chain.py's own report, the one most likely to be read as "is anchoring healthy", never surfaced the split that would have shown the gap either way.

Fixed going forward in commit 5197ac273707de53cfe25a26d82a3d6a8186c679. nightshift/anchor_ots.py: the skip-check now looks for the PRESENCE of a confirmed attestation instead of the ABSENCE of a pending one -- the correct completeness signal, since one calendar confirming is sufficient regardless of whether others are still pending. core/verify_chain.py: now reports confirmed, pending, and stale-pending (more than 24 hours old, mirroring self_audit.py's existing OTS_GRACE_HOURS constant) as three separate numbers instead of one lumped "receipted" count. Detection uses two attestation tag byte sequences -- PendingAttestation.TAG and BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation.TAG, taken directly from python-opentimestamps's own notary.py -- searched for structurally in the raw proof file's bytes. This keeps verify_chain.py stdlib-only with no `ots` CLI or subprocess dependency, matching its existing zero-repo-imports design and its own stated honest limit: this confirms the proof file embeds a Bitcoin-attestation structure, not that that attestation's block header and merkle path actually check out against the real blockchain -- `ots verify` against a real node is still the deeper check. Cross-validated against the real `ots info` CLI on a random 40-file sample of this repo's actual receipts: 0 mismatches. The nightly sweep's schedule and 30-second budget are unchanged; this is a logic fix, not a retuning.

The backlog itself was cleared by a one-off manual catch-up sweep immediately after the fix -- same code, a longer single uninterrupted run, no change to the production schedule or budget. Before: 143 confirmed, 193 pending, 191 of those stale. After: 336 confirmed, 0 pending, 0 stale. 193 receipts were upgraded. Two of them raised a TimeoutExpired on their first attempt during the sweep (a 25-second subprocess limit against a slow calendar response) and were not left as a silent gap: both were retried individually immediately afterward and succeeded on the very next attempt, resolving instantly from the calendar's cache. Zero receipts in this entire backlog proved structurally unable to upgrade -- every failure encountered was a transient slow-calendar timeout, not a dead or permanently-unconfirmable receipt.

No backfill: entries 1 through 346 stand exactly as published, unedited. This is a disclosure plus a forward fix to tooling, not a correction of any chain entry's own content -- anchor_ots.py and verify_chain.py are the record's anchoring and reporting tools, not chained payloads themselves. Neither touched file sits on the frozen strategy_version surface (nightshift/strategy_version.py's STRATEGY_VERSION_FILES does not list either), confirmed before committing; no strategy_version move was made or needed. Verified with seven new tests in tests/test_anchor_ots.py, all subprocess calls mocked so none hit a real calendar: the core regression (an already-confirmed proof must never be re-attempted), a genuinely pending proof is attempted and its success logged, an unupgradeable-this-run receipt stays pending without crashing or being deleted, an unreachable calendar's TimeoutExpired is caught and logged with the sweep continuing to the next file rather than aborting, a corrupted file's `info` failure is skipped rather than crashing the sweep, time-budget exhaustion stops cleanly and logs it, and main() with no `ots` binary installed at all exits 0 and logs plainly without touching anything. tests/test_verify_chain.py was extended for the new confirmed/pending/stale schema, including a cross-check that the two attestation tag constants agree with what this repo's real receipts actually contain. All three suites pass together: test_anchor_ots.py 7/7, test_verify_chain.py 16/16, test_publish_chain.py 9/9 (run for regression, unaffected by this change). core/verify_chain.py reports CHAIN VALID throughout, 346 entries unbroken from genesis, and now shows 336 confirmed / 0 pending / 0 stale where it previously showed a single undifferentiated 336 receipted.

payload.description:
Discloses a new input-archive mechanism: a corpus-delta archive (nightshift/archive_corpus.py) and a pinned Python interpreter version (.python-version), the first two of the three-item minimum set a prior scoping session identified for making a published call independently reproducible by a third party -- raw OHLCV bars, a derivatives/signals snapshot, and the full corpus delta (every candidate that passed MC gating, not just the one published). The third item, raw OHLCV, is deliberately not built here; see below.

Why this was urgent: corpus.db -- the SQLite store nightshift/cycle.py's insert_config_entry() writes every MC-gate-passing candidate into, and the table the meta-model trains its ranking on -- is gitignored and has always existed only on the operator's own machine, listed explicitly under ".gitignore"'s "local backups & regenerating artifacts -- never commit." That's the right call for corpus.db itself, a derived SQLite index. But it means the entire training set behind the meta-model's ranking decision -- which candidate becomes the published call on a given night -- has never existed anywhere verifiable. Six labeled dates from graduation, the record's headline claim becomes "the meta-model is live," and the data it was trained on would have been invisible, unbacked, and on one laptop. This closes that gap before graduation rather than after.

What was built: nightshift/archive_corpus.py runs after each night's cycle completes (wired into run_and_publish.sh, between run_nightshift.py succeeding and the brief being chained) and reads back, from corpus.db, every row inserted under that night's cycle_id -- every config that passed all 5 MC gates, whether or not it became the published call -- appending each as a canonical JSON line to reports/archive/corpus_delta.jsonl, an ever-growing append-only file in the same spirit as reports/predictions.jsonl. nightshift/publish_chain.py now hashes that whole file into every chained entry (corpus_delta_n, corpus_delta_sha256), the identical reference-by-hash pattern predictions_n/predictions_sha256 already use. The derivatives/signals snapshot the scoping report separately named as a second item turned out to need no separate mechanism at all: the five scalars (funding_rate, oi_trend_7d, exchange_flow_7d, longshort_ratio, btc_dominance_delta) are already columns on every corpus.db row, so archiving the corpus delta archives the signals snapshot for free.

Design choices, stated plainly. Every completed cycle gets exactly one cycle_marker line, even on a night where zero candidates passed MC gating -- deliberately, so a reader can never confuse "this night has not been archived yet" with "this night genuinely produced nothing," the same reasoning PIPELINE_FAILURE entries exist for at the chain level. A cycle that crashed before completing gets no marker at all, because there is nothing in corpus.db for it to represent, and that night's failure already has its own honest PIPELINE_FAILURE chain entry; inventing a second place for the same fact to live would only give it a second place to go stale. Every run scans for every completed cycle with no marker yet and backfills all of them in one pass, oldest first -- the same defer-and-sweep shape as nightshift/anchor_ots.py's OTS backlog sweep and run_and_publish.sh's own push_or_defer(), so one bad night (disk full, a locked database, a permission error) is caught up automatically by the next successful run rather than silently lost. No backfill, as instructed: the archive begins at cycle_id 20261007, the first cycle to run after this shipped. The 589 corpus rows this project had already accumulated before today are not retroactively dumped into the archive -- the record says plainly, by the absence of any earlier cycle_marker, that entries before this have no archive.

One scope limit is worth stating up front rather than discovering later: this archives each corpus row exactly as it existed at insert time. nightshift/db.py's update_live_outcome() mutates a row in place weeks afterward, once a deployed config's live performance is actually graded (live_sharpe_20d, decay_ratio, survived, and related fields) -- those later mutations are not re-archived by this version. A reader of this archive sees the corpus precisely as the meta-model would have seen it when it made that night's ranking decision, not any row's eventual real-world outcome. Reproducing the meta-model's training input for a given night is fully covered; reproducing a full live-performance-updated view of the corpus as it stands today is not, and would need its own separate append-only trail of outcome-update events.

The frozen-strategy-surface question was checked before anything was committed, as required. None of the five touched or added files -- nightshift/archive_corpus.py, nightshift/publish_chain.py, nightshift/self_audit.py, run_and_publish.sh, .python-version -- appear in nightshift/strategy_version.py's STRATEGY_VERSION_FILES list. strategy_version is confirmed unchanged at 06d869d35c9922053016cd0b316ea5ceffc6b58906239dbbe2e12e65359887e5, before and after. This was achievable because everything the corpus-delta archive needs is already written to corpus.db by code that already exists (cycle.py's own insert_config_entry() calls); reading it back afterward, from a standalone script in the same category as self_audit.py and anchor_ots.py, touches nothing on the frozen surface. The third item in the original minimum set, raw OHLCV, does not have this escape hatch: the exact closed-bar window a prediction was actually made against is only available at two points in the codebase -- nightshift/cycle.py's Stage 1 fetch, or nightshift/stamp_prediction.py's _context_hash() call site, which receives and hashes that identical window -- and both of those files ARE on the frozen strategy surface. An archive built instead from an independent re-fetch, from outside the freeze, would not be guaranteed byte-identical to what was actually hashed that night: exchange-side data revision or simple timing drift could produce a slightly different window, and an archive that might not match the thing it claims to verify would be worse than no archive at all -- actively misleading rather than closing the gap. So raw OHLCV archiving was not attempted in this pass. Whether the strategy_version move is worth it is explicitly left as the operator's decision, not made here.

nightshift/self_audit.py gained one line: archive_corpus.py was added to ENTRY_POINT_SCRIPTS so check 4 (dead_code_reachability) recognizes it as a standalone, separately-invoked script rather than flagging its own top-level calls as unreachable from cycle.py's call graph -- the same accommodation self_audit.py and anchor_ots.py themselves already have. Verified directly, calling both checks before and after this commit: dead_code_reachability still flags exactly 17 symbols (unchanged), doc_reference_integrity still flags exactly 2 (unchanged). This work introduces no new self-audit findings of its own -- worth stating given the self-audit visibility gap disclosed in this same record's history.

Verified with eight new tests in tests/test_archive_corpus.py, built against a real throwaway SQLite database constructed through nightshift.db's own init_db(), log_cycle_start(), log_cycle_end(), and insert_config_entry() -- not hand-rolled SQL, so these tests will themselves break if the real schema or those functions' contracts ever drift, rather than silently testing against a stale assumption. Covered: the happy path (a marker plus every candidate line for a night with real candidates); a completed night with zero passing candidates still getting its marker with zero candidate lines; an incomplete, crashed cycle getting no marker at all; the no-backfill cutoff being respected for a cycle_id before the archive's start; an idempotent second run adding nothing new; the sweep correctly catching up several missed nights in a single pass; a simulated disk-full write failure returning cleanly without raising and being picked up automatically on the very next, unmocked run; and a corrupted existing archive file being treated as covering zero cycles rather than crashing the script. tests/test_publish_chain.py gained four more cases for the new _corpus_delta_snapshot() function and its wiring into append_entry(), covering both a missing and a present archive file. All four suites pass together: test_archive_corpus.py 8/8, test_publish_chain.py 13/13, test_anchor_ots.py 7/7, test_verify_chain.py 16/16. core/verify_chain.py reports CHAIN VALID throughout.

The honest limits carried forward from the original scoping report, verbatim, because the feature's name must not be allowed to imply more than it delivers: this archive proves that a given byte sequence was committed to this chain at a given time, under a given code_version -- the same guarantee every other hash-chained, OpenTimestamps-anchored entry on this record already carries, no more and no less. It does not prove that any upstream exchange actually served the exact bytes a future raw-OHLCV archive would contain -- that piece isn't built yet, and when it is, it will prove what was committed and when, not that Binance served those exact bytes; that remains a trust assumption in the operator who committed them, exactly as it already is for every context_hash on this chain today. It does not prove that the code which actually executed on a given night was, in fact, the exact commit that night's code_version names -- code_version records which commit should have produced that call, not independent proof that the running process matched it. And a call being fully reproducible from this archive would not make it a sound one: reproducibility and correctness are separate claims, and nothing here closes the gap between them.

This move was approved explicitly, in these words: breaking a freeze while the slice is n=18 costs less than breaking one that has become the headline number -- done deliberately ahead of the meta-model's n=30 labeled-date graduation threshold, not after.

The prior slice's record is kept intact, exactly as every previous repoint on this chain already keeps its predecessor. In core/verify_chain.py, the constant that governed the freeze through the third correction is renamed from FROZEN_STRATEGY_VERSION to FROZEN_STRATEGY_VERSION_V3 -- its value is unchanged, its filter is unchanged, and its filtered return-stats section is neither edited nor removed, only relabeled from "current frozen strategy version" to "superseded; kept for history", matching the exact wording every earlier superseded generation already uses. A new FROZEN_STRATEGY_VERSION constant and its own frozen_strategy_version_return_stats section now start fresh at n=0 win / n=0 loss, governing from this correction forward. The module now tracks five freeze generations, not four; its docstring was updated to describe this fourth correction in the same detail as the first three.

What was built: nightshift/archive_ohlcv.py's archive_closed_bars(asset, closed, source, cycle_date), called from the exact point described above. It is not a re-fetch -- the whole reason this had to touch the frozen surface, rather than being built as an external standalone script the way the corpus-delta archive was, is that the exact bytes a prediction's context_hash commits to exist nowhere outside that one in-memory DataFrame at that one call site; an independent re-fetch from outside the freeze could not be guaranteed byte-identical to what was actually hashed, which would have made the archive misleading rather than verifying anything, as the prior scoping report already concluded. It writes to an ever-growing reports/archive/ohlcv.csv.gz, appending a new gzip member per archiving call -- concatenated gzip members decompress back into one continuous stream when read, the same way log-rotation tooling appends to .gz files, so the archive stays appendable without ever touching bytes already flushed. Each closed bar becomes one CSV row: cycle_date, asset, bar_date, source, open, high, low, close, volume. Every float is written via Python's own repr(float(x)) -- the shortest decimal string that parses back to the exact same 64-bit float, not a rounded or truncated value -- so a verifier who re-parses an archived row and rebuilds nightshift/stamp_prediction.py's hash payload from it reproduces the identical context_hash, not an approximation of it. The frozen-strategy-surface question was checked before anything was committed, as required, and the answer this time is different from the corpus-delta work: nightshift/stamp_prediction.py is on nightshift/strategy_version.py's STRATEGY_VERSION_FILES, and this change edits it directly, deliberately, and as minimally as the design allows. nightshift/archive_ohlcv.py itself is not on that list and never will need to be: it only reads the `closed` object it's given, never mutates it, and has zero effect on what stamp() returns -- non-causal to the signal, by the identical reasoning nightshift/derivatives.py was already traced out of the frozen surface despite being imported by nightshift/cycle.py. Verified directly before and after this commit: self_audit.py's dead_code_reachability check still flags exactly 17 symbols, unchanged -- archive_closed_bars, its internal log(), and its internal _already_on_disk() are all correctly recognized as reachable through the normal call graph via stamp(), since this is an ordinary library module rather than a standalone script, and needed no ENTRY_POINT_SCRIPTS accommodation the way archive_corpus.py and self_audit.py itself do. doc_reference_integrity still flags exactly the same 2 pre-existing findings. This work introduced no new self-audit findings of its own.

The code_dirty exclusion question was asked directly and confirmed, not assumed: reports/archive/ was already added to nightshift/publish_chain.py's RUN_OUTPUT_PATHS during the corpus-delta work, and because that exclusion is a directory pathspec (":!reports/archive") rather than a file-specific one, it already covers reports/archive/ohlcv.csv.gz with no separate entry needed. This was verified two ways: directly, by creating a throwaway file at that exact path and confirming `git status --porcelain` against the same pathspec set reads it as clean; and permanently, with a new test, test_ohlcv_archive_falls_under_the_same_reports_archive_exclusion, added to the existing CodeVersionDirtyScopeTest suite in tests/test_publish_chain.py.

No backfill, visible immediately in two places. This very disclosure entry's own ohlcv_archive_n is null, with ohlcv_archive_read_error stating the file does not exist yet -- the archive has no content at all until the next real nightly cycle stamps a real prediction and the file is created for the first time. And every night before this commit has no OHLCV archive whatsoever; the chain says so plainly by the same absence entry 348 already demonstrated for the corpus-delta archive's own beginning, not by any special-cased claim.

One honest limit is specific to this archive and does not apply to its two siblings, and is worth stating precisely rather than glossing over: the "defer and sweep" property that lets a failed corpus-delta write or a failed OTS stamp be recovered on a later run does not fully extend here. corpus.db's rows persist on disk regardless of whether last night's archiver run succeeded, and an existing-but-unconfirmed OTS proof can always be re-upgraded on a subsequent sweep -- both have something durable to come back to. This archive's raw material, the `closed` DataFrame, exists only inside the memory of the one cycle process that fetched it. The only recovery this mechanism offers is a within-run retry: if a different candidate for the same asset comes up later the same night, it gets a free second attempt, because archive_ohlcv.py never marks a failed write as done. But if every candidate for a given asset fails to archive on a given night -- a disk that stays full the whole run, say -- there is no later sweep that can retrieve that exact window again, because the only way to get it back would be a re-fetch, and a re-fetch is precisely the thing this module exists to avoid relying on. A night where this happens is a real, permanent, and honestly visible gap: that night's ohlcv_archive_n simply does not grow, discoverable by its own absence rather than hidden by a false claim of completeness.

With both the raw OHLCV bars and the corpus delta now archived -- the latter disclosed in the entry immediately before this one -- a third party can, for the first time on this record, independently re-derive a published call for any night from this commit forward, not merely verify that an entry wasn't edited after the fact. What that would actually take: this repository checked out at the exact code_version commit the target chain entry names; the exact pinned Python interpreter from .python-version together with `pip install -r requirements.txt`, every dependency already pinned with an exact `==`; that night's archived raw OHLCV rows from reports/archive/ohlcv.csv.gz, filtered by cycle_date and asset, used in place of a live Binance fetch; and that night's archived corpus-delta rows from reports/archive/corpus_delta.jsonl, filtered by cycle_id, standing in for what corpus.db held at that moment, to reproduce the meta-model's training input for that night's ranking decision. No exchange API key and no live network access of any kind would be required -- the archived inputs now fully substitute for both the price fetch and the corpus read that a live run would otherwise need. Given those inputs, re-running the pipeline's deterministic stages -- regime classification, walk-forward optimisation through a TPESampler seeded at 42, Monte Carlo gating through an RNG seeded at 42, and meta-model training and ranking through an estimator seeded with META_SEED -- and diffing the resulting selected call against what predictions.jsonl actually recorded for that date should produce a match, not merely a resemblance, since every stochastic step in this pipeline already runs from a fixed seed. What is not yet built, and is not being claimed as done by this entry, is the verification script or command itself -- something that would mechanically re-run a given night against its archived inputs and report whether the result matches what was published. This entry closes the data side of third-party reproducibility; writing the tool that actually performs that re-derivation and comparison remains separate, future work.

The honest limits from the original scoping report are carried forward here verbatim, because archiving the data must not be allowed to imply more certainty than it actually delivers. This proves that a given byte sequence was committed to this chain, at a given time, under a given code_version -- the same hash-chain and OpenTimestamps guarantee every other entry on this record already carries, no more and no less. It does not prove that Binance actually served these exact raw bytes: this archive proves what was committed and when, not that Binance served those exact bytes -- that remains, and will always remain, a trust assumption in the operator who committed them. It does not prove that the code which actually executed on a given night was, in fact, the exact commit that night's code_version names: code_version records which commit should have produced that call, not independent proof that the running process matched it. And a call being fully reproducible from these archives does not make it a sound one: reproducibility is not soundness, and nothing built across either of these two disclosure entries closes the gap between the two.
