payload.description:
Discloses core/reproduce.py -- the reproduction verifier -- and the results of running it for real against 2026-10-07, before this entry, per the instruction that no disclosure would happen until it was known whether the tool actually reproduces a real night. Three findings, kept separate deliberately because they are three different kinds of claim: one success, one significant pre-existing gap the archive exposed rather than created, and one open question not yet answered.

Finding one: reproduction works, where it was tested against matching inputs. core/reproduce.py replayed regime classification, walk-forward optimisation, and Monte Carlo gating against only the archived closed-bar window for 2026-10-07 -- no exchange account, no API key, and no network access of any kind; the script never imports ccxt or any network-capable module, and a monkeypatched socket guard that would raise loudly on any real connection attempt never fired. Of the 17 configs that passed all 5 MC gates in that replay, 12 were rediscovered from the momentum and relative strategy families with an exact config_id match -- momentum 7 of 7, relative 5 of 5. config_id is a content hash, sha256 over {asset, strategy_family, params} as defined in nightshift/wfo_engine.py's _config_id(), so an identical config_id is proof that the exact same hyperparameters were found, not approximate agreement rounded to a few decimal places. A TPESampler seeded at 42, run on a different machine at a different time, working from nothing but the archived bars, found the identical optimum the live run found that night, for those 12 candidates. Separately, nightshift/stamp_prediction.py's _context_hash() was recomputed from the archived bars for all three assets -- BTC/USDT, ETH/USDT, SOL/USDT -- and matched the hash predictions.jsonl actually recorded, exactly, in every case. Both results required nothing beyond this repository and its archived files.

Finding two is the significant one, and it predates the archive entirely: the archive captures the window that gets hashed, not the window that actually produced the call, and this has been true since _context_hash() was written, not since the archive was built. nightshift/stamp_prediction.py's _context_hash() hashes `closed` -- the fetched window with today's in-progress daily candle excluded, bars through yesterday only. But nightshift/cycle.py's regime classification, the WFO and MC-gate inputs, the entry-signal computation, and the entry_price calculation all use the FULL fetched window from Stage 1, today's live candle included. context_hash has therefore always described a narrower input than the one that actually produced that night's call. The archive did not create this discrepancy -- it exposed it, by finally giving something concrete to diff the decision against. Three downstream effects were traced to this one cause in the 2026-10-07 replay, not three separate problems: regime classification came out one day stale, because nightshift/regime_engine.py's rolling features treat their last row as "today," and the replay's last row was actually yesterday's; entry_price was taken from yesterday's close instead of today's live price, because entry_price is literally closes[-1] and the replay's closes array ends one day earlier than the real run's did; and BTC produced no call at all on replay, despite its exact winning configuration -- BTC/USDT_momentum_c1417f344a4c -- being rediscovered with byte-identical parameters, because entry_signal() evaluated one calendar day in the past returned "none" instead of "long" for that same config. That BTC case is the clearest demonstration that this is a data-completeness gap and not a determinism failure: the optimizer found the exact right answer from the data it was given; the data it was given was simply the wrong day.

Finding three is an open question, not a closed one, and is reported as such rather than dressed up with an unverified explanation. None of the five breakout-family WFO survivors from the replay matched the real run's by config_id -- zero of five, every one a different set of discovered parameters. The one-bar archive gap from finding two was checked directly as a candidate explanation for this and does not account for it: WFO's fold boundaries were computed by hand for both 499 bars (what the archive holds) and 500 bars (what the real fetch had), and they are identical in both cases -- neither the training slice, which maxes out around day 453, nor the out-of-sample scoring slice, which maxes out around day 488, ever reaches far enough back to touch the missing bar at index 499. Momentum and relative share this exact same fold logic and matched exactly, which is consistent with the one-bar gap being irrelevant to WFO's own search in this case. What's left is a hypothesis, stated as a hypothesis: breakout_params() defines a conditional search space, where exit_lookback's upper bound (max(6, lookback // 2)) depends on the same trial's own sampled lookback value -- a shape that is known to be more sensitive to how TPESampler's history-based proposal distributions break ties than an independent parameter space is. Several of the replayed SOL/USDT breakout candidates converged to an identical Sharpe ratio of 5.875 despite carrying different parameter values, which is consistent with this particular dataset having several near-tied optima that a conditional search can land on differently depending on some difference not yet identified -- but that is a hypothesis to investigate, not a diagnosis, and it is disclosed as unresolved. None of the calls actually published on 2026-10-07 were breakout-family, so this did not affect that night's record, but it remains an open determinism question for any future night where a breakout call is the one that gets published.

Verified before committing core/reproduce.py: it is not in nightshift/strategy_version.py's STRATEGY_VERSION_FILES, so this addition did not touch the frozen strategy surface and strategy_version is confirmed unchanged at 2dd2221ce744f26e5dad3367a080a118329f22c9020860a0e950c2797985fee0. nightshift/self_audit.py's ENTRY_POINT_SCRIPTS gained one entry for reproduce.py -- without it, the network-blocking guard's nested callback (assigned to socket.socket.connect rather than called by name) was flagged by check 4's name-based reachability walk, exactly the getattr/callback-assignment false-positive class that check's own docstring already names. With the entry added, dead_code_reachability still flags exactly 17 findings and doc_reference_integrity still flags exactly 2, both unchanged by this commit. All 60 existing tests continue to pass, and core/verify_chain.py reports CHAIN VALID throughout.

payload.description:
Discloses two changes together: a throughput redesign of the OTS upgrade sweep, and --splice-live-candle (Option B), a new opt-in capability in core/reproduce.py. They land in one entry because both were diagnosed and built in the same session and the sweep's real numbers are short enough to state plainly alongside the splice's constraint, but they are three separate findings and are kept separate below rather than blended into one narrative.

First, the sweep's real before-numbers, stated precisely rather than summarized away. Since the 2026-10-06 one-off catch-up that cleared that day's backlog, the nightly upgrade sweep ran 11 times and upgraded zero entries in every single one of those runs, each time hitting its 30-second budget before completing. Measured directly: with 357 total receipts on disk, the then-current (and, as of the 2026-10-06 fix, correctly-written) skip-check cost roughly 161 milliseconds per file in pure `ots info` subprocess overhead -- 57.6 seconds to walk the full candidate list, which exceeds the 30-second budget outright. Candidates were tried oldest-mtime-first, so the budget died at file 181 of 357 on every run, never once reaching any of the 18 genuinely pending entries, all of which -- being the most recently stamped -- sat at the tail of that ordering. This was checked directly for genuine upgrade failure before assuming otherwise: `ots upgrade` was run directly, with no budget limit, against three of those eighteen stale entries (chain entries 347, 355, and 364), and all three succeeded on the first attempt, in four to five seconds each. The cause was confirmed to be throughput, not failure, before a single line of the fix was written. Throughout this entire eleven-run stretch, the hash chain itself was never affected -- core/verify_chain.py reported CHAIN VALID the whole time; only the confirmed-versus-pending breakdown of OTS coverage was degraded, and that breakdown is itself a feature disclosed only days ago specifically so a gap like this one would be visible rather than silently folded into a single "receipted" number.

The fix changes the sweep's shape, not its budget -- UPGRADE_TOTAL_BUDGET_S stays at 30 seconds, unchanged, as instructed. A new file, nightshift/logs/ots_confirmed.index, gitignored and local-only, holds a flat set of entry hashes already known to be Bitcoin-confirmed. Checking an indexed hash is now a Python set lookup -- no subprocess call, no `ots info`, nanoseconds instead of milliseconds -- so the sweep's cost is proportional to how many receipts are not yet indexed as confirmed, which in steady state is a handful of recent, genuinely pending entries, not the full history of every receipt this chain has ever produced. This cache is deliberately not a second source of truth for anything: a Bitcoin attestation that has confirmed never becomes unconfirmed again, which is the property that makes a simple "once true, forever true" cache safe in the first place, and core/verify_chain.py and nightshift/self_audit.py each continue to inspect the real .hash.ots file bytes directly, independently, every time, never reading this index at all. If the index file is missing or unreadable, it is treated as empty and rebuilt from the receipts themselves over the course of that run -- logged, never raised -- which is exactly the "rebuildable from the receipts themselves if lost or corrupted" property that was required of whatever mechanism got used here. One more change was needed to make this actually work rather than just move the same bug to a different budget ceiling: candidates not yet in the index are now tried newest-first, reversed from the previous oldest-first order. Oldest-first was a reasonable choice when every file was re-checked every single run regardless of its state, since an old, long-confirmed file cost exactly the same skip-check as a brand new one and deferring newer, more-likely-still-pending files to the end of the run was harmless. It is not reasonable now: on the very first run after this fix ships, or on any future run after the index has been lost and is being rebuilt from scratch, every file is briefly unindexed at once, and oldest-first would walk the entire long-confirmed prefix before ever reaching the genuinely pending entries -- reproducing the identical bug this fix exists to close, just under a different name. Newest-first means a cold or rebuilding index costs only a one-time, budget-bounded indexing pass over old entries that are already confirmed and in no particular hurry, while the entries that are actually pending -- which, by construction, are always the most recent ones -- get tried first on every single run, whether the index is cold or warm.

This was measured for real, not just reasoned about. A cold run, with no index file existing yet at all, took 32.2 seconds and upgraded eight real entries in that one run -- more than the previous eleven runs combined, which upgraded zero. Seven total runs of this kind fully indexed and cleared the entire backlog: 357 of 357 receipts confirmed, zero pending, zero stale. An eighth run, now against a fully warm index, completed in 0.047 seconds, logging plainly that all 357 receipts were already confirmed and indexed and there was nothing left to check. That is the committed state of reports/ots/ in this entry's underlying commit: twenty-one receipt files are now committed as genuinely Bitcoin-confirmed on disk -- the three upgraded by hand during diagnosis (347, 355, 364) plus eighteen more cleared automatically by this fix's own cold-start catch-up pass -- closing the inconsistency of a receipt sitting confirmed on disk while the published chain still called it stale.

Second, and unrelated to the sweep: --splice-live-candle, a new opt-in flag for core/reproduce.py implementing the "Option B" design discussed after the first real reproduction run against 2026-10-07 disclosed a genuine, pre-existing gap -- nightshift/stamp_prediction.py's _context_hash() hashes `closed`, the window with today's in-progress candle excluded, but the real cycle's regime classification, WFO and MC-gate inputs, entry-signal computation, and entry price all come from the full fetched window, today's live candle included. The idea behind Option B is that a given night's live candle becomes the very next archived night's own last CLOSED bar, one calendar day later, once that day has actually finished -- so it can be recovered from there instead of being archived twice or re-fetched. Provenance is verified before any bar is trusted, not assumed: the next night's own context_hash is recomputed from its archived bars and checked against what that night actually recorded -- reusing the exact same verification function the base night's own integrity check already uses -- before a single value is pulled out of it. Four distinct, specifically worded refusal paths exist, and there is no silent fallback to the closed-only window in any of them: a same-day or future target date is refused as out of scope by definition, since the following night hasn't run yet; a missing archive for the following night is refused by name; a following night that stamped zero predictions at all is refused with that specific, separately diagnosed reason, since it is expected to be a common and entirely legitimate real occurrence rather than a symptom of a malformed archive; and a following night whose own context_hash fails to verify against its archived bars is refused outright, because an archive that does not verify against what it itself recorded is not trustworthy enough to borrow from regardless of what it contains. A narrower, asset-level gap -- one asset's bar missing from an otherwise fully verified next-night archive -- is logged and that one asset is left at its original closed-only length, rather than aborting the entire run over a single asset.

This was run for real, against the real 2026-10-07/2026-10-08 pair, before this disclosure, exactly as asked. The result was a refusal, and the refusal is the correct, working result, not a failure to report around: "night 2026-10-08 stamped zero predictions -- every candidate that night had no entry signal." This was confirmed directly against nightshift/logs/cycle_2026-10-08.log, which shows twelve configs passing MC gating that night and all twelve logging "no entry signal tonight" -- archive_closed_bars() is only ever called from inside stamp(), after the direction-is-"none" check, so zero predictions stamped that night means it was never called for any asset, and there was genuinely nothing for the splice to recover. The plain constraint this exposes, stated here rather than left for a reader to discover by hitting it unexpectedly: the splice only works across two CONSECUTIVE prediction-stamping nights, which is a narrower condition than "any night that has an archive at all." 2026-10-07 into 2026-10-08 is not such a pair, and this entry does not pretend otherwise. The feature ships with this real-run refusal as its recorded evidence of correct behavior; it will be retested the next time two consecutive nights both stamp at least one real prediction, and is not being forced or faked today to manufacture an earlier success.

Verified before committing either change. tests/test_anchor_ots.py grew from 7 to 14 cases, covering first-encounter indexing, zero subprocess calls on a second run against an already-indexed hash, a still-pending entry deliberately left unindexed (indexing a "not yet" would make that answer permanent), a missing or corrupted index degrading to empty and rebuilding rather than raising, newest-first ordering, and a mixed indexed/unindexed candidate set. tests/test_reproduce.py adds 8 new cases built against a real gzip archive member and a real predictions.jsonl row whose context_hash comes from the actual _context_hash() function, so the happy path is checked against real verification logic rather than a mocked stand-in for it. payload.description:
Discloses a structural defect found by direct code reading, not inference: the meta-model's graduation gate checks a counter that has been permanently zero since the gate and the counter both existed, which means train() has never once been invoked from the real nightly pipeline and the meta-model could not have graduated at 30 labeled dates, or at any other count, regardless of how many nights have run. This entry is the disclosure alone, published first and separately as instructed, before any code is touched.

The causal chain was traced start to finish. nightshift/meta_model.py's MetaModel.should_retrain(), in its pre-training branch, returns `labeled_date_count() >= META_MIN_SAMPLES` to decide whether train() should even be attempted for the first time. nightshift/db.py's labeled_date_count() counts `COUNT(DISTINCT outcome_date) FROM corpus WHERE survived IS NOT NULL AND void_reason IS NULL` -- it depends entirely on the corpus table's survived column actually being set. That column is written only by db.py's update_live_outcome(), which is called only from meta_model.py's collect_pending_outcomes() -- itself run every night from cycle.py's Stage 2 -- but collect_pending_outcomes() skips every single row it's given unless that row's config_id appears as a key in the `live_performance` dictionary it's handed. That dictionary comes from cycle.py passing self.monitor.live_performance_snapshot(), nightshift/live_monitor.py's LiveMonitor.live_performance_snapshot(), which is derived entirely from self._active. self._active is populated only by LiveMonitor.register() -- and register() has zero callers anywhere in this codebase, confirmed directly by grep across every Python file in the repository, a fact already disclosed separately, in passing, inside nightshift/strategy_version.py's own comments about why meta_model.py sits on the frozen strategy surface as a conservative buffer. This was verified against the real database, not left as a theoretical conclusion: corpus.db holds 633 total rows as of this entry, and precisely zero of them have survived set to anything other than null. labeled_date_count() therefore evaluates to zero, corpus_size() likewise evaluates to zero, and every one of should_retrain()'s pre-training checks reads a counter that cannot move, by construction, independent of how many nights run or how many predictions get graded by label_outcomes.py in the meantime.

The direct consequence: train() has never been invoked from the nightly path, at all, since this project began. The only other call to MetaModel.train() anywhere in this repository is inside run_nightshift.py's --demo subcommand, which seeds a synthetic corpus with fabricated rows via numpy's random generator and calls train(force=True) against that fabricated data for demonstration purposes -- it is not part of the nightly pipeline that run_and_publish.sh invokes with no flags every night, and it has never been. cycle.py's own call site, `if self.meta.should_retrain(self.cycle_id): ok = self.meta.train()` at Stage 6, is simply never entered under real nightly operation, because should_retrain()'s pre-training branch is permanently False. self._trained has therefore never once become True outside of the --demo path. The meta-model could not have graduated at 30 labeled dates or at any other count. This was true from the very beginning of this project's real nightly operation, not a recent regression and not something that broke -- nothing changed recently to cause it, and nothing recent is needed to explain it. LiveMonitor.register() has had zero callers since the day it was written, by all available evidence, and labeled_date_count() has had this exact relationship to should_retrain() for exactly as long.

The brief has, this entire time, been displaying a different, genuinely real, and climbing number with no wiring whatsoever to the gate described above. cycle.py's _brief() formats a line reading "Corpus: {n} distinct labeled dates -- ACTIVE" or "-- STANDBY, need 30 dates" depending on whether db.py's labeled_prediction_date_count() -- a count of distinct settle_date values among predictions.jsonl rows that label_outcomes.py has graded against real closing prices -- has reached 30. That counter is real, live, structurally unrelated to labeled_date_count(), and currently stands at 27, climbing at the ordinary nightly grading rate. Nothing connects this counter to should_retrain() at all. The consequence, not yet observed because the count has not yet reached 30 but on the current trend plainly on its way there: once labeled_prediction_date_count() crosses 30, a future night's brief would print its META-MODEL section header as ACTIVE -- that header's wording is driven solely by this one counter -- while self._trained remains false, because should_retrain() never fired on the other, permanently zero counter, and every individual configuration's own META line that same night, via MetaRankScore.explain(), would still read "[FALLBACK] corpus too small -- using GT-Score=...". A single brief, self-contradicting itself between its own header and its own body, was on a clear path to being published with nothing in the pipeline positioned to prevent it or even notice it happening.

This was already being detected, correctly, every single night, and nothing ever read it. nightshift/self_audit.py's check 4, dead_code_reachability, has flagged live_monitor.register() as unreachable from nightshift/cycle.py's call graph in every one of the 70 AUDIT_RESULT entries chained so far, starting with chain entry 21 on 2026-08-01 -- the very first night that check ever ran. That is 70 of 70, not 67 of 67; the lower figure reflects an earlier count taken a few nights before this entry, and three more nightly audits have chained in the interval, each one still flagging the identical finding, without a single lapse in either tally. The check has been correct and working for ten full weeks. Nothing in this pipeline, and nobody looking at it, acted on what it was already saying. This is the second time a correctly functioning check on this record has reported into a complete void: the first was the OTS anchoring backlog, disclosed in chain entry 347, where self_audit's own ots_proof_coverage check had independently reported FAIL every single day since 2026-08-01 while nothing downstream of that check ever acted on it either. Both findings sat in a report that was being generated correctly, every night, and simply was not being read, until a routine status check happened to open it.

No backfill. No prior chain entry is edited, corrected, or reinterpreted by this one. Every NIGHTLY_BRIEF published before this entry stands exactly as it was originally published, including any night whose labeled_prediction_date_count was already approaching 30 while the meta-model remained, unmentioned in that night's own brief header, un-trained. This entry discloses the mechanism behind that gap; it does not retroactively relabel any night's record as having said something different than what it actually said. Two further questions this finding directly raises -- which counter should actually gate graduation, and whether a graduation event should itself be chained -- are deliberately not answered by this entry. They are being reported as analysis only, with no code touched, separately from this disclosure, exactly as instructed: this entry ships the finding alone, first.

payload.description:
METHODOLOGY_CHANGE: meta-model graduation gate repointed off a permanently-dead counter (should_retrain() fix, nightshift/meta_model.py + nightshift/cycle.py).

Disclosed in entry 381: should_retrain()'s pre-training branch gated on labeled_date_count(), which counts corpus.survived -- written only via a call chain ending at LiveMonitor.register(), which has zero callers anywhere in this codebase. That made the gate permanently unable to open, from the beginning, against any amount of real data. It now gates on labeled_prediction_date_count() instead.

The gate sat above two layers that were already correct. train()'s own internal gate (n_dates = labeled_prediction_date_count(); n_dates < META_MIN_SAMPLES) and _df()'s actual training rows (get_prediction_labeled_corpus()) were both already reading the live, prediction-graded source -- only should_retrain() itself, the thing deciding whether to call train() at all, was still reading the dead one. Fixed by repointing should_retrain()'s pre-training branch to labeled_prediction_date_count(), the exact counter those two layers already used.

The post-training branch had the same defect and was fixed in the same pass. Its 20%-growth retrain trigger compared against corpus_size(), which depends on the identical dead corpus.survived column and is therefore also permanently zero. Fixing only the pre-training branch would have graduated the model once, the first time the gate happened to open, and then retrained it only on the fixed META_RETRAIN_EVERY cadence -- never again on growth, silently, for the same reason the gate itself never opened. The growth check now reads len(get_prediction_labeled_corpus()) against the trained n, live.

This landed three labeled dates before the milestone it unblocks. At the time of the prior disclosure (entry 381), the real counter stood at 27 of the META_MIN_SAMPLES=30 required for graduation. Uncorrected, within roughly a week -- the pace at which labeled dates have been accumulating -- the counter would have crossed 30 while should_retrain() kept reading the dead one: the nightly brief's progress line would have printed ACTIVE off the real, climbing count while every individual config line still printed "[FALLBACK] corpus too small," because rank()'s model_active flag depends on self._trained, which depends on train() having actually been called, which depends on the gate this fix repoints. The timing is part of what makes this worth disclosing now rather than after the fact: this is not a defect found long after it mattered, but one found while there were still three labeled dates of runway to fix it before the brief and the gate would have visibly disagreed.

This moved strategy_version (nightshift/meta_model.py and nightshift/cycle.py are both on the frozen 8-file surface) -- disclosed and repointed separately in core/verify_chain.py (2dd2221ce744... -> 0abecbf74ce8..., sixth generation). It is a gating fix, not a change to how a call is made: no change to entry_signal(), direction, entry_price, or which config gets ranked or selected. The prior slice (FROZEN_STRATEGY_VERSION_V4, 3 wins / 3 losses) is kept intact, filtered and printed as superseded, same treatment as every prior repoint.

Graduation itself is now a named event on the chain. The moment should_retrain() opens for the first time and train() succeeds (the fallback -> trained transition, not a routine retrain), nightshift/cycle.py writes a sidecar and publish_chain.py's new --graduation flag publishes a dedicated METHODOLOGY_CHANGE entry carrying n_train, cv_auc, cv_r2, which counter opened the gate and its value, and the trained model's feature importances. It fires once, on the transition only; routine retrains afterward do not re-trigger it.

A side effect worth naming directly rather than leaving implicit: self_audit.py's dead_code_reachability check's total count is unchanged at 17, but its composition is not. feature_importances() (nightshift/meta_model.py) was flagged unreachable in every run for roughly the same ten-week window disclosed for register() in entry 381 (since checks began, 2026-08-01) -- the graduation sidecar this fix adds now genuinely calls it, so a function dead for ten weeks is, as of this change, load-bearing in the entry that announces the model's own graduation. That fixed false positive is exactly offset by a new one: labeled_date_count() (nightshift/db.py) is now flagged, because should_retrain() was its only caller and no longer calls it. It is left defined, deliberately, not deleted -- it is the correct gate for a live-deployment pipeline that does not exist yet (LiveMonitor.register() is still never called), not a mistake. If that pipeline is ever wired up, this is the function that gate should use, and should_retrain() is the method that would need revisiting again at that point, deliberately. The audit's total staying at 17 is coincidence, not evidence that nothing changed.

No backfill. Prior briefs and chain entries stand as published.

METHODOLOGY_CHANGE: dead_code_reachability's 17 flagged findings triaged to zero, and audit findings now routed to the watchdog's off-machine alert path.

Two self_audit.py findings were detected correctly and read by nobody: the OTS backlog climbing 4 to 191 over 66 days, and live_monitor.register() flagged unreachable in all 70 of 70 self-audits since checks began (2026-08-01) -- which was the graduation bug disclosed in entries 381/382. The checks worked every night. There was nowhere for the output to land, and the standing 17-finding count never looked different from the night before.

Audit routing. nightshift/watchdog.py now diffs tonight's AUDIT_RESULT chain entry against the one immediately before it and alerts on CHANGE, not standing level: a check that newly fails when it passed before, a finding count that increased on an already-failing check, a check that newly passes again (routed at lower priority -- worth knowing, not worth the same tone), and entries_without_ots_proof climbing (a top-level count on the payload, not one of the per-check finding lists, which is exactly how the OTS backlog grew for 66 days without ever being compared night over night). Routed through notify_offmachine(), the same delivery-checked, logged channel disclosed in chain entry 256, extended with an optional priority parameter that defaults to "urgent" for every pre-existing caller. The baseline is the chain itself -- the last two AUDIT_RESULT entries -- not a separate state file; nothing new to lose, nothing to rebuild.

dead_code_reachability's 17 were triaged into four categories, reported before any of this was implemented.

A scan-scope gap, not an AST blind spot (2 symbols). run_nightshift.py is the actual nightly entry point -- run_and_publish.sh invokes it directly -- but it lives at the repo root, outside every directory this check's AST_SCAN_DIRS named, and was never added to ENTRY_POINT_SCRIPTS either. The checker had never parsed the one file that calls nightshift/meta_model.py's top_features() and corpus_health(). Both were flagged dead in all 70 of 70 audits since checks began (2026-08-01) -- the same window, same count, as live_monitor.register()'s false "unreachable" wasn't, this one actually was invisible by construction, not by any dict-dispatch or callback blind spot. Fixed by adding run_nightshift.py to AST_SCAN_EXTRA_FILES (by file, not by directory -- the repo root also holds tests/ and venv/, which stay correctly out of scope) and to ENTRY_POINT_SCRIPTS. Verified directly, before committing: with the gap closed, the flagged count dropped by exactly these two symbols and nothing new surfaced. A scanner that misses the entry point could in principle also be missing other symbols reachable only through it; checked for that specifically, and found none.

A documented suppression table, two categories kept visibly distinct (10 + 4 symbols). DEAD_CODE_SUPPRESSED in self_audit.py is checked before a symbol is added to the flagged list; suppressed entries move to detail["suppressed"], visible with an explicit category field, not silently dropped. AST_BLIND_SPOT (10 symbols) means real, live code the checker structurally cannot see being called: the eight functions nightshift/cycle.py dispatches through STRATEGY_REGISTRY["family"]["fn"/"param_space"] (a dict subscript, never an ast.Call node), _safe_ret() which only those eight call (unreachable here purely as a second-order consequence of the same blind spot), and wfo_engine.py's objective(), passed by reference to optuna's study.optimize(objective, ...) rather than called directly -- a different blind spot than dict dispatch, same conclusion. DELIBERATELY_DEAD (4 symbols) means genuinely unreachable right now, kept on purpose: labeled_date_count() and get_labelled_corpus() (nightshift/db.py, both dependent on corpus.survived, written only via LiveMonitor.register(), which has zero callers), and LiveMonitor.register() and LiveMonitor.add_return() themselves (nightshift/live_monitor.py) -- the live-deployment pipeline these would wire up was never built. "Confirmed live, checker's blind spot" and "actually dead, kept on purpose" are different claims, and a reader can now see which is which without opening the source.

The table audits itself. _audit_suppression_table() runs every audit and flags two ways the table itself can go stale: a suppressed symbol no longer existing in the scanned source at all, and a DELIBERATELY_DEAD symbol the checker now finds reachable -- meaning it may have gained a real caller, and the "kept for a pipeline that doesn't exist yet" justification needs re-examining rather than being trusted forever. Both surface as findings on the suppression_table_issues key, counted toward this check's own status. Without this, the suppression table would become exactly the next place a real regression goes to hide -- the same failure shape this whole task exists to fix, one level removed.

One genuine deletion. get_all_signals() (nightshift/derivatives.py) was a thin wrapper, fully superseded by get_all_signals_with_status(), which nightshift/cycle.py has always called directly. Its only caller anywhere was tests/simulate_all.py, a manual smoke-test script outside this check's scan scope, updated to call get_all_signals_with_status() directly instead.

dead_code_reachability now reports zero flagged findings and zero suppression-table issues -- the first time since checks began on 2026-08-01 that this check has reported zero, and the first time a zero from it means something: every one of the 17 symbols that used to sit under the standing count has an explicit, individually-checked disposition (fixed, suppressed-and-justified, or deleted), not an absence of looking.
